AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVES
AbstractText.content: This study aims at evaluating the chronic disease risk related to prolonged work in long-hour schedules for eight major chronic diseases: heart disease, non-skin cancer, arthritis, diabetes, chronic lung disease, asthma, chronic depression, and hypertension.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: The study used data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth, 1979 covering 32 years of job history (1978 to 2009) for 7492 respondents. Logistic regression analyses were performed to test the relationship between average weekly work hours, and the reported prevalence of those conditions for each individual.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Regularly working long hours over 32 years was significantly associated with elevated risks of heart disease, non-skin cancer, arthritis, and diabetes. The observed risk was much larger among women than among men.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Working long-hour schedules over many years increases the risk for some specific chronic diseases, especially for women.
